Aerosol scattering between stars and planets has been detected via photometric dips in stellar light over the past decade, offering a novel method for characterizing interplanetary and interstellar aerosols. This technique holds significant value for both celestial and terrestrial atmospheres, complementing existing methods like mass spectrometry and lidar, which each possess specific limitations. By applying statistical optics to analyze dip distributions, we can determine optical depths and size distribution parameters. Notably, the distribution of dips among relatively bright stars in a field is exponential; the associated "characteristic dip depth," representing the depth where 37% of stars remain unaffected by scattering, allows for direct calculation of the medium's optical depth. We demonstrated this approach with a study of interplanetary aerosols at 550 nm during the ARTEMIS satellite's final eclipse pass, deriving an optical depth of $1.8 \pm 0.3$ and validating the size distribution with concurrent lidar data. Looking ahead, observing characteristic dips in stellar fields during total solar eclipses could provide the most accurate optical depth measurements during solar events. Additionally, extrastellar photometry during planetary events (e.g., Venus transits) could yield the most precise constraints on the size distribution. In this paper, we will present updated results from the ARTEMIS event incorporating data from a wider field of view and more stars, explore potential applications during solar events and planetary alignments, and discuss future possibilities for examining extraterrestrial dust clouds. Automated systems generating image captions are routinely assessed using public reference datasets, with performance measured by overlap-based metrics like BLEU (Bellemare et al., 2014), BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2018), or G_eval (Li et al., 2018). The fundamental flaw in this methodology is that no existing dataset guarantees the grammatical correctness or factual accuracy of its human-written captions. Consequently, there is a risk that models optimize for overlap metrics without aligning with the true quality of image descriptions. To investigate this, we created a 100-point quality scale by having 250 professional annotators rank the best and worst captions for 20 images from Flickr8K (Hildebrandt et al., 2017). We examined how this scale correlates with BLEU-4, G_eval, and BertScore when applied to images from Hashtag8K (Mohand-Ousaada et al., 2019), discovering that the scales do not follow the same trend. Furthermore, we trained a regression model on the Hashtag8K dataset to predict our 100-point scale from image text using a 60/20/20 train/validation/test split. The model achieved a Mean Absolute Error of 13.14 and a Spearman rank correlation of 0.5018 on the test set. These results indicate that while the regression predictions are not perfectly accurate, they provide a more reliable estimation of descriptive quality than traditional overlap metrics like BLEU. Our findings suggest that future image description tasks should utilize direct quality assessment over reliance on proxy metrics such as BLEU. To support this shift, we release the 8K dataset on our website at https://sites.google.com/view/desquality8k/home. This resource comprises 8,000 images with three caption alternatives each, designed for selecting the most appropriate image description. Our dataset will be particularly valuable for evaluating descriptive quality in low-resource scenarios, such as the newly introduced CO-COOP 2027 dataset, and for training models via metric learning using best-of-3 approaches (Ivanovic et al., 2022). Additionally, it can serve as a foundation for multi-task learning models aimed at both predicting rankable image descriptions and regressing a numerical quality score (Bhagavatula et al., 2020).

Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) demands a rigorous statistical approach to ensure reliable extraction and, crucially, meaningful error estimation and hypothesis testing. While numerous groups perform these fits using diverse methodologies, error calculation often relies on ad hoc techniques lacking solid theoretical grounding. This is particularly problematic given the rapid expansion of uncertainty ranges when incorporating higher-order terms. Furthermore, existing methods struggle to handle "mild" constraints, such as those from PDF sets with varying assumptions about high-x behavior or unmeasured processes used for extrapolation. Our proposed framework addresses these issues by systematically integrating all source characteristics—data type, uncertainty, and constraints—along with the specific technique used for each. Within this structure, we treat members of an ensemble (e.g., from a particular data subset) as carrying both probability density information and explicit error estimates, the latter derived via any consistent method, whether statistical or non-statistical. Leveraging recent advances in Monte Carlo simulation, we implemented this framework in AirFit, making it accessible through the fast and versatile Monte Carlo module LiAPeX. We demonstrated AirFit's capabilities and versatility with the CT18 dataset, which included over 50 processes and three distinct determination methods. The results confirm that traditional approaches like "reweighting" and "expansion" can yield error estimates comparable in size to those from direct fitting, with consistency across methods. Additionally, we extended the dataset with processes featuring large uncertainties to create the CT18+ set, successfully characterizing their errors and observing increased uncertainties in the resulting PDFs as expected. AirFit is available at https://github.com/CTeq/AirFit.

This study employs direct numerical simulation (DNS) to analyze a turbulent non-premixed jet flame subjected to acoustic forcing. Within a linearized framework, the response is decomposed into reflected and transmitted components, while the flame's reaction to this oscillating velocity field is modeled using an active flame approach to close the system of equations. Derived theoretically, this reaction is simulated numerically via precomputed lookup tables. To validate the model's ability to capture flame dynamics, an alternative method for introducing oscillations is utilized, for which the linearized response is calculated directly. Results from both techniques align closely, confirming the approach's efficacy. Subsequently, the model is used to investigate how initial conditions and specific flame characteristics influence oscillatory behavior. Furthermore, the lookup table generation process is adapted to simulate frequency variations, revealing that the reaction amplitude follows a resonance curve. Finally, the model is applied to explore the impact of inflow turbulence intensity and heat release on the response, demonstrating that higher turbulence levels and increased heat release generally amplify the reaction amplitude. Ultimately, this work illustrates how a linearized model can examine flame responses across varying frequencies and parameters, offering insights into behaviors that would be difficult to assess directly through DNS. While this research focuses on an unconfined jet, the methodology is universally applicable to any flow configuration; in that context, it serves as a powerful tool for analyzing flames in complex geometries and assessing their reactions to acoustic or other disturbances. Nonlocal gravity models serve as effective frameworks for investigating the gravitational collapse of ultra-dense matter without requiring modifications to Einstein's general relativity. These models become essential when the mean free path of photons and other particles within an ultra-dense fluid approaches the fluid's scale height, causing the gravitational field to depend on energy density in a nonlocal manner. To date, only one model has achieved a constitutive formulation suitable for numerical implementations: the formal nonlocal gravity (FNG) model. We present a comprehensive review of nonlocal gravity, beginning with an overview of various nonlocal theories from other physical domains. Subsequently, we detail the derivation of the FNG model's constitutive relation and introduce a generalized nonlocal gravity (GNG) model that extends FNG by incorporating multiple relaxation times associated with different relaxation processes. Our derivation confirms that the FNG constitutive relation results from the special case of a single relaxation time within the GNG framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both the FNG and GNG models yield identical predictions when applied to ultra-dense matter where only one dominant relaxation process—either photon or neutron mean free path—occurs. We anticipate that the proposed GNG model will prove valuable for analyzing nonlocal gravitational effects in matter with multiple mean free paths, such as neutron star material. Building on this, we will derive the field equation for the GNG model in our upcoming work. Additionally, we compare the FNG and generalized fluid dynamics models, highlighting their shared mathematical structure despite differing physical contexts. Finally, we outline several unresolved issues in the FNG and GNG models and address them through the development of a novel nonlocal gravity model in our future research. In the immediate term, we will utilize the FNG model to derive a nonlocal hydrodynamic constitutive relation for ultra-dense matter, which will then be employed in joint collapse simulations based on the GNG model. Such simulations will also require accounting for radiative transfer and neutron beta decay processes; meanwhile, the nonlocal hydrodynamic relation will be incorporated into these simulations via a kinetic theory approach. Our long-term goal is to assess the validity of general relativistic simulations of neutron star collapse and formation through the nonlocal gravity model employed in those simulations. Such an evaluation could potentially reveal that nonlocal gravity effects prevent the formation of singularities inside collapsing neutron stars, thereby challenging the necessity of quantum gravity theories motivated by singularities in black holes or ultra-dense matter. Statistically significant A/B testing is essential for determining if the performance differences between two algorithms differ significantly from the overlap in errors between those algorithms. The paired-permutation test is a non-parametric method that requires an immense number of simulations to achieve high statistical significance. To facilitate this, we introduce a precise paired-permutation test for structured test statistics using an exact algorithm. Our approach is significantly more efficient than conventional paired-permutation tests, achieving at least an order of magnitude greater precision within the same computational timeframe. Furthermore, our method is flexible enough to convert any conventional paired-permutation test targeting a specific level of significance into the exact precision provided by our algorithm. We evaluate our algorithm against the conventional n-vs-n parallel random process in both isolated and distributed environments. The results demonstrate that our algorithm reaches the same level of significance with far fewer computational resources, efficiently utilizing the entire available computational power of a computational grid.

For any finite classical group $G$ acting on a space of dimension at least 3, the complement of the set of regular elements (or, in the unitary case, the elements with trace at least $-1$) within $G$ forms a complex of codimension 2 geodesic subgraphs, defined by the collection of non-regular elements (or, for unitary groups, those with trace $\geq$ -1). This paper examines the topological structure of this complex and demonstrates that it is homotopy equivalent to a product of circles and a additional codimension 1 subgraph, which corresponds to the complex of singularities for the action of $G$ on the projective space. Furthermore, the article analyzes the topological features of this complex of singularities, specifically in the context of the alternating and symmetric groups. The complex of codimension 2 subgraphs formed by derangements within the symmetric and alternating groups is also investigated, with its topological properties derived from those of the overall complex of non-derangements. These investigations yield a set of conjectures regarding the topological characteristics of the complex of non-derangements for the symplectic and orthogonal groups. Additionally, the topological features of the complex of codimension 2 subgraphs consisting of elements with exactly one cycle of length greater than 1 within the classical groups are also studied. All of this work extends the generalization of the "fundamental group method" to the symmetric, alternating, and classical groups. As a result of applying this method, explicit descriptions of the first homotopy group and of higher homotopy groups for the complex of regular elements in each finite classical group have been achieved. These findings, along with those from prior literature, confirm that the complex of non-derangements in any finite classical group is homotopically a product of circles.

In the context of semi-Metric space, a timelike curve $\gamma(s)$ parameterized by arc length is classified as a timelike Bertrand curve if its tangent indicatrix in the causal Minkowski plane $\E_2^1$ possesses the identical geometric definition as that of its derivative curve $\alpha(s)$, also a timelike curve with unit speed. This work establishes the fundamental properties of timelike Bertrand curves within semi-Metric space and introduces the concept of a dual timelike Bertrand curve. It is demonstrated that a timelike curve $\gamma(s)$ in semi-Metric space is a timelike Bertrand curve if and only if it is a (dual) timelike $\alpha$-curve, characterized by the relation $|\kappa(s)| = a|\tau(s)| + b$ where $a,b\in\R$, is superimposed with a (dual) timelike $\beta$-curve, defined by $|\bar{\kappa}(s)| = A|\bar{\tau}(s)| + B$ where $A,B\in\R$, through the condition $|\bar{\kappa}(s)|\kappa(s) = a|\bar{\tau}(s)|\tau(s) + bB - AB$. Furthermore, it is proven that every timelike Bertrand curve in semi-Metric space admits a unique dual representation that is also a dual timelike Bertrand curve. The proofs rely heavily on the Inversion Theorem and the Superposition Theorem of differential geometry in semi-Metric space. Additionally, it is shown that a timelike curve $\gamma(s)$ is a dual timelike Bertrand curve if and only if its associated (dual) timelike $\alpha$-curve and (dual) timelike $\beta$-curve are both dual timelike Bertrand curves. Finally, various examples of such curves are constructed. Throughout this study, the formula method is utilized to derive these results. These findings offer a foundational framework for future investigations into the theory of timelike Bertrand curves in semi-Metric space. Among the most critical hyperparameters for neural networks, the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. To facilitate this, we developed a unified framework capable of integrating any loss function with any neural network architecture; the corresponding open-source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/AbdulKhaleque/KLD_ICT}. We hope this framework encourages further research into loss functions beyond cross-entropy, helping to establish it as a prominent hyperparameter in future studies. Ultimately, our results confirm that the "best" function is not universally optimal but depends entirely on the specific dataset and problem at hand.

The metric dimension of a graph $G$, denoted by $\dim(G)$, represents the smallest size of a resolving set for $G$. When evaluating how closely $\dim(G)$ aligns with the standard graph invariants—specifically the diameter $\mathcal{D}(G)$, order $n(G)$, and order minus one, $n(G)-1$—it becomes evident that $\dim(G)$ can substantially exceed $n(G)-2$. This inactivation phenomenon typically occurs in graphs featuring a high-degree vertex connected to a long path. In practical applications, such topologies are often optimized away using trimming operations. This paper investigates the impact of this optimization on resolving sets by introducing the concept of metric dimension for trimmed graphs. We establish lower bounds for this parameter within the class of trimmed trees and determine the exact values for specific families of paths and broom-like structures. Furthermore, we define a family of graphs called "broomsticks," for which we calculate the metric dimension across both trimmed and untrimmed variants. These calculations reveal that the metric dimension of a "broomstick" can remain invariant under trimming unless the graph is a "bare" broomstick, a configuration that corresponds to a full path. In such cases, the dimension is one greater than what is possible for a path of equivalent diameter, highlighting the significant influence of a vertex's degree on this invariant. Consequently, we derive an upper bound for the metric dimension of a trimmed tree $T$ as a function of its diameter. Finally, we identify a family of trees where this bound is achieved, precisely characterizing the metric dimension of a trimmed tree in terms of its diameter and maximum degree. These findings also clarify the characteristics required for a tree to possess the maximum metric dimension relative to its diameter. Regarding the order of a resolved graph (whether trimmed or not) given its metric dimension and diameter, we provide the corresponding formulas for a trimmed path.

We demonstrate that for the ASEP with step initial conditions and particle ranks restricted to a Gaussian speed range, a central limit theorem holds concerning the fluctuations of velocity along the characteristics. Consequently, this process exhibits non-Lipschitz behavior, indicating chaotic dynamics. To establish this result, we introduce and utilize a novel approach: deriving a limit shape theorem from a central limit theorem (which follows via a functional version of the method of moments). Specifically, we prove the central limit theorem for velocity fluctuations along characteristics, assuming additionally that higher-order fluctuations remain tight. Subsequently, in the spirit of [20], we derive a shape theorem from a central limit theorem for an associated gradient process. Finally, applying the argument from [2, 19], we conclude the reverse direction: a central limit theorem follows from the shape theorem. The proof of the main theorem relies on the fact that, as noted in [1], the velocity process converges to an Anderson–Cohen–Glasser process under the same conditions.

Mathematical models of epidemic evolution serve as essential tools for analyzing the dynamics of pathogen spread and testing potential control strategies. While significant research has been conducted on models for the current SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, there remains a risk of prioritizing complex formulations without sufficient consideration for the practical utility of their outputs. This article provides a review of models developed up to date for the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, emphasizing the necessity of validating results against observed data. We also examine key characteristics of the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic and its progression, highlighting the challenges in forecasting its course and evaluating control measures. Although simple models effectively captured the initial epidemic curve of SARS-CoV-2 in Italy, they failed to anticipate the subsequent rise in infections following the first lockdown. Furthermore, we analyzed models designed to assess the efficacy of specific interventions, as well as those integrating meteorological variables and human mobility metrics to better predict the epidemic's trajectory. Ultimately, no single model has successfully incorporated all relevant factors to accurately forecast the epidemic's evolution; however, these efforts have clarified the critical variables involved. Given the limitations of current models in anticipating the rise of infections after Italy's first lockdown, further investigation into the underlying drivers of this increase is required. Additionally, as nations like Italy prepare to relax certain restrictions, models must be capable of evaluating these new protocols to guide informed decision-making.

To address these issues, we implemented a simple model of the SFM trajectory turnover driven by gas sequestration, incorporating the fraction of nidal stars formed post-sequestration, into the  Illustration  II hydrodynamic simulation. The model's predictions were then compared against the turnover's shape observed across the  Illustration  II boxes and against observed M*-SFR data points, with the latter's turnover operationalized as the transition between low- and high-mass data sets. Our findings indicate that a nidal star-formality of approximately 10$^{-9}$ yr$^{-1}$ and a sequestration efficiency of 10$-$20% are required to replicate the turnover's shape within the  Illustration  II boxes. Once sequestration efficiency exceeds 25%, the resulting SFM trajectory flattens or downturns at masses lower than those corresponding to the observed turnover. The star-formality of the most massive galaxies simulated ($\gtrsim$$10^{11}$$M_{\odot}$) aligns more closely with observations above the low-mass cutoff ($fSF\sim$$10^{-8}$yr$^{-1}$) than below it ($fSF\sim$$10^{-9}$yr$^{-1}$), supporting the validity of our model within the simulated volume. Fake news spreads rapidly and perversely through social media, with deepfides—authentified multimedia misinformation—becoming increasingly common. Despite the massive volume of data, effective detection models require frequent domain exposure, a constraint that meta learning addresses by generating robust classifiers from few shots. However, cross-domain few-shot learning, essential for fake news detection, remains challenging because it demands sufficient support-set examples to identify categories. This paper introduces MEPND, a novel multimodal meta-learned neural process network. Unlike traditional approaches, MEPND can detect fake news categories in a target domain without requiring any labeled examples for those categories, even when no historical data exists. Evaluated on real-world datasets, our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in mean accuracy for five-way and ten-way classification tasks. Furthermore, MEPND successfully identified a recent, previously unseen deepfake category from the PAWS dataset, confirming its power in identifying emergent fake news. The source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/Pranav-106/Multi_Emergent_Fake_News_Detection.

Golay regular cross arrays (GRCAs) are multiport array antennas composed of two regular cross arrays with complementary directional characteristics, finding significant application in dual- and multi-port radio systems such as cognitive radio, MIMO, and SDMA. Similarly, the Golay regular polygon array (GRCPA) consists of three or more Golay regular polygon arrays with complementary properties, offering a novel multiport antenna structure with potential for various radio applications. This study introduces a new three-port array configuration based on Golay complementary sequences, termed the Golay triscendental regular array (GTRCA). Building upon GTRCA, we propose a three-port array structure called the Golay Triscendental Regular Array (GTRA), which is derived from GRCAS and GRCPPAs. Specifically, this structure integrates one Golay regular cross array (GRCX), one Golay regular pentagon array (GRCPE), and one GTRCA. We demonstrate that GTRA maintains a flat gain pattern by combining GRCX, GRCPE, and GTRCA, and provide the mathematical formulation for calculating the information rate of GTRA. To enable the implementation of GTRA, we design a multi-stage polyphase network for GTRCA. Consequently, a specific instance of GTRA with a information rate of 7.5 is realized using antenna elements of unit cost. Finally, we validate a further GTRA example with an information rate of 9, constructed from unit-cost elements, confirming its feasibility through a multi-stage polyphase network design.

Synthetic data serves as an effective strategy to expand limited datasets, helping to preserve privacy and preventing data overuse. Furthermore, this paper argues that generated data can function as a "domain adaptation" tool, enabling models trained on real data to achieve higher accuracy when classifying previously unseen injured brain CT images. To accomplish this, a Progressive AVAE architecture is developed to produce CT scans of sound brains from those showing injury. Since damaged brains exhibit complex deformation patterns, a progressive training approach is necessary to ensure high fidelity in the output. Once the model is trained, it requires no further configuration; it can directly process injured brain images to generate corresponding "sound" images, which serve as the target domain for an AI model trained to distinguish between sound and injured brains using only sound brain data. Experiments conducted on public CT datasets demonstrate that the Progressive AVAE yields superior fidelity compared to other GAN and VAE models when converting injured to sound brains. Additionally, a neural network trained on a dataset of sound brains and the proposed Progressive AVAE-generated injured brains achieved 96.06% accuracy, surpassing the 94.79% accuracy of a model trained exclusively on the complete original mixed data. Finally, the Progressive AVAE proves effective against data manipulation attacks; when generating images from adversarially perturbed injured CTs, the system produces fewer errors than seen in similar tasks with other GAN models. Directly creating defensible AI systems for analyzing injured brain CTs remains challenging, but the Progressive AVAE offers a viable solution, potentially serving clinical, legal, and forensic applications. The source code and data for the Progressive AVAE are available at: https://github.com/Dr-Siddharth-Shah/PROGRESIVE_AVAE_Brain_Injury.

Feature extraction is a crucial preprocessing step in deep learning systems designed for specific tasks. This research proposes a contrastive learning-based framework that unifies the selection of appropriate pre-trained models for specific applications. UNIFY (Unified Structure for Feature Extraction based on Contrastive Learning) begins by contrasting a target task with its source task to embed a task-specific encoder, drawn from a library of encoders compatible with the objective, into an end-to-end contrastive learning network. This network is initially trained on data from the target task (which is fully supervised) and the source task (unsupervised) to establish contractions between positive pairs and expanding contractions between negative pairs within the same source task samples. The proposed contrastive loss function simultaneously optimizes the selection of the most suitable pre-trained encoder and fine-tunes it for the specific target task. UNIFY was evaluated on two text classification datasets and one semi-supervised graph node classification dataset. Results indicate that this simple yet effective method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches for both supervised and semi-supervised learning, successfully selecting and fine-tuning an optimal pre-trained model for each specific task without requiring manual intervention. The UNIFY system is accessible at https://github.com/ElhamGh01/UNIFY-.ixx.

Although large language models (LLMs) are primarily trained using massive text corpora, recent studies indicate that incorporating structured knowledge—such as knowledge graphs—can further enhance performance. This paper presents a method to integrate skills, defined as task-specific knowledge graphs, into LLMs to boost natural language understanding and generation. Our approach consists of two stages: first, we condition the model on a global embedding of the entire skill graph; second, we provide in-context examples pairing natural language queries with the condition (graph embedding) and the desired output. Evaluations show that with as few as three examples per query type, our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art zero-shot and few-shot techniques across six diverse datasets. Furthermore, this framework requires no dataset-specific tuning and effectively handles multi-hop reasoning. The open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/IBM/LLM-Skills.

Non-linear electric fields are incorporated into the mass–charge phase plane of extended unified transformation laws (EUTOL) to examine the thermodynamic connections between the horizon, causal, and energy complexes. While the horizon complex yields a traditional analysis utilizing the Clausius equation, this study focuses on the causal complex to derive a Landsberg distance, thereby establishing a non-linear Landsberg equation within the causal framework. Furthermore, investigation into the energy complex reveals that the Bochner curvature tensor vanishes solely at equilibrium; consequently, the Bochner curvature is employed to explore the first-order phase transition between large and small black holes via the chemical potential. Finally, the Landsberg curve, energy complex, and Bochner curvature tensor are examined across the charge range ($0\le Q\le 0.5$) for both extreme and near-extreme black holes. These analyses highlight how non-linear field strengths influence the shape of the causal curve in the temperature–charge plane and modify the fluctuations of the first-order chemical potential within the energy complex. These findings offer fresh insights into the fluctuations of black hole thermodynamics. Additionally, the EUTOL framework is validated against the first law for non-linear charged AdS black holes, and a comparative analysis of the Landsberg curve, temperature, and heat capacity is conducted for both AdS and Schwarzschild black holes. The results indicate that the non-linearity of the Reissner-Nordström (RN) charge exerts a more significant effect on the curve's shape than on the heat capacity. These conclusions suggest that the unity of the EUTOL framework persists even in the context of AdS black holes.

If $G$ is a classical or exceptional simple Lie group acting on the multiplicity-free module $M$ composed of all harmonics for a specific rank $d$, we construct the lattice of submodules of $M$ using only the dimension function and the $G$-invariance of candidate submodule sums of multiplicities. This construction is achieved through a classical linear algebraic process applied to the function $\dim(V\otimes M)$ for a classical Lie group $G$ and a submodule $V$ of $M$. Consequently, we derive the Witting inversion formula, which allows us to determine the multiplicity of any submodule from its dimension, and we establish that for classical simple Lie groups, this lattice is atomic and complemented. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when $G$ is of type $A_n$, the submodule lattice corresponds to the lattice of multiplicities of elementary symmetric functions, and if $G$ is of type $B_n$ with $n\ge 3$, it aligns with the lattice of multiplicities of $h$-Catalan functions (for $d-1\ge n$), as defined by Simion. In Euclidean space, a submanifold deemed minimal possesses minimality recurrentness when its recurrent behavior—defined as the decomposition of curvature into a 1-form and a tensor—coincides with that of its mean curvature vector. This concept has been extensively examined across various contexts. The authors begin by establishing that no non-lightlike minimal submanifolds with dimension at least three exhibit recurrentness in Minkowski space. They then investigate biharmonic submanifolds within the Euclidean space that are not constant, focusing on their "mean biharmonic recurrentness." Specifically, they analyze this property in Euclidean spaces of dimensions five through eight, proving that any such submanifold in $\mathbb{R}^5$ must be an isoparametric hyper surface with exactly two distinct principal curatures. Finally, they explore the same concept in $\mathbb{R}^6$, demonstrating that a mean biharmonic recurrently minimal submanifold with at most three principal curvatures and no flat normal bundle in $\mathbb{R}^6$ must be a hyper surface in $\mathbb{R}^6$ possessing two distinct principal curvatures.

This study tackles the significant difficulty in establishing reliable statistical regularities from non-Gaussian noise distributions. Using a straightforward experimental setup, we investigated the force required to peel an adhesive tape at a constant speed from various surfaces. The resulting noise distributions show that surface roughness drives non-Gaussian behavior, which aligns with a noise generation mechanism tied to local peeling rates across surface asperities. Furthermore, we found that the standard deviation of the force follows a power law relative to the applied speed, indicating that hysteresis in the local force-speed relationship responsible for noise also scales with speed. Notably, this power-law exponent matches the exponent governing the transition from stick-slip to smooth sliding friction observed in other systems. Finally, we provide evidence for regularity in the local force response to speed and derive a corresponding distribution of local damping coefficients. These results support the conclusion that chaotic dynamics do not cause the noise; rather, it originates from the local force response to velocity fluctuations across surface asperities. The overall findings support the hypothesis that the physical processes governing frictional noise during sliding are identical to those producing crackling noise during peeling. Additionally, the data indicates that local force regularity during sliding is at least as fragile as the statistical regularity of the global force, a finding with significant implications for the detection of precursors to sudden slip events in seismology and other systems exhibiting crackling noise. Specifically, this suggests that the lack of regularity in force fluctuations during the steady sliding of seismic faults—an issue already recognized in laboratory studies of rock samples—may stem from the superposition of local slip-sliding noise across fault surface asperities, similar to what occurs in adhesive tapes. Such local noise could potentially be reduced by increasing fault surface smoothness, as demonstrated with adhesive tapes. Such an approach might also be beneficial for minimizing noise in seismic monitoring following major earthquakes to facilitate more accurate post-event earthquake prediction. Additionally, reducing local slip-sliding noise could enhance the detection of precursors to sudden slip events, whether during seismic aftershocks or in industrial applications involving sliding components, such as the gears in the LIGO gravitational wave detector. We conclude by discussing these potential applications and by addressing the regularity of local force and velocity fluctuations during the stick-slip motion of asperities.

Furthermore, the TPC architecture lacks robustness against adversarial attacks and geometric transformations such as rotation and scaling. Automated testing serves as a crucial final safeguard against subtle errors in source code, playing a significant role in enhancing software reliability. This paper introduces a geometric method for verifying correctness in compiled C/C++ programs, a technique that can also refine automated testing workflows. Specifically, this approach identifies potential mismatches between actual program outputs and anticipated results, categorizing them into two types: semantic errors, which indicate logical failures where outputs deviate from expectations, and geometric errors, which pinpoint locations of nondeterministic behavior causing output variations. The system isolates these errors to guide developers, while also offering an interactive visual environment to explore execution traces and pinpoint the exact source of discrepancies. Besides assisting in debugging incorrect tests, this capability aids in refining the correctness criteria themselves. Implemented as an additive tool named RegTest (available at https://github.com/RegTest/RegTest), it works seamlessly with existing compilers and compilers-compatible debuggers, requiring no modifications to the test code or its surroundings. Empirical results from both industrial and academic cases demonstrate that RegTest successfully identifies flawed tests and invalid correctness specifications, with successful runs offering insights into how to align non-deterministic behaviors with intended outcomes. The application of this tool in industry to correct errors in a C# test suite (utilizing a comparable approach) is also discussed. Furthermore, the method was employed to guide experiments with a formal verification tool on an embedded system's test suite; these experiments revealed that errors in a hand-written test remained difficult to fix manually, whereas RegTest effectively highlighted the specific aspects needing adjustment. Finally, this geometric-based error localization aligns with end-to-end testing strategies used to validate formal methods, such as those in Coq. RegTest serves as a valuable utility for software engineers, particularly when cooperating with formal verification systems, and can function as a precursor to model checkers by narrowing down potential issues in test suites before they undergo formal assessment.

This paper presents a novel proof of the existence of Hilbert--Blum--Riemann weights for GL_2 over number fields with characteristic Serre weights that are Hodge--de Rham in the clean range, utilizing Kummer theory. The author demonstrates that this new approach requires fewer assumptions on the residual weight than the method based on de Rham weights, as evidenced by the necessary conditions in Theorem 1.1 and Definition 2.1. Furthermore, the study establishes a connection between the existence of Hilbert--Blum--Riemann weights and the solvability of certain p-adic De Rham character conditions, arguing for the utility of employing de Rham theory over number fields to investigate automorphic forms and representations in the characteristic 0 category. Finally, the work introduces existence and uniqueness criteria for these weights within the context of Tate spaces.

This study introduces a novel framework for precise damage shaping in self-sensing composite materials via electrical impedance tomography (ZIT) and genetic algorithms. While self-sensing composites, particularly carbon-fiber-reinforced polymers (CFRP), enable non-contact damage detection through methods like scanning microwave radiometry, their automatic localization does not ensure controlled damage for applications in material shaping, repair simulation, or damage simulation. Utilizing a genetic algorithm, we mapped the nonlinear relationship between carbon fiber tows' orientation during manufacturing and the resulting material's electrical impedance tensor measured by ZIT. Concurrently, an optimization process determined the optimal tow arrangement to achieve specific damage shapes after non-destructive testing, ensuring exact shape precision. This approach was validated experimentally on a uniaxial composite panel and a complex curved double-cantilever beam, confirming the method's efficacy in achieving targeted damage shapes. These findings offer a controlled manufacturing technique for creating distinct damage patterns in self-sensing composites, facilitating detailed investigations into damage localization, simulation, and repair using advanced non-destructive testing methods. Keywords: Self-sensing composites, carbon fiber reinforced polymer, damage shaping, electrical impedance tomography, genetic algorithms, damage localization, NDT, NDT. We introduce a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces that prioritizes coordinate-independent formulations, explicitly separating geometric vectors from the mathematical tools used to handle them. This distinction allows us to clarify the role of the "hat" operator and its variants, which convert vectors into bivectors, and to establish a basis for defining additional operators with identical functionality. Within this framework, we systematically develop a system of vector identities and a set of "triple" identities specifically designed for tensor equations involving the "hat" operator. To support this, we also define a corresponding system of identities for the cross product. All proposed identities are illustrated through multiple examples that demonstrate their application. Finally, we extend this approach by introducing an operator that maps a vector and a tensor of rank $n$ to a new tensor of rank $n-1$, utilizing this tool to formulate identities for these operators as well. These identities facilitate the simplification of expressions containing the operator, and several examples highlight their utility. As a final demonstration, we construct a coordinate system where the "hat" operator acquires a simplified representation. This construction relies on a specific decomposition of the space into two subspaces, a method we also generalize to create frameworks for simplifying tensors in other coordinate systems based on similar subspace decompositions. Throughout this work, we deliberately avoid utilizing the formalism of orthogonal coordinate systems. Our system of vector identities serves as a valuable supplement to standard sets found in literature, proving particularly useful for simplifying expressions that blend tensors with geometric vectors and other mathematical constructs. Similarly, our coordinate system, which utilizes an orthonormal basis to distinguish between "special" and "ordinary" vectors without imposing further constraints, offers a flexible approach for analyzing tensors in Euclidean spaces. This flexibility extends to bases that are orthonormal in a generalized sense, allowing for investigations into coordinate systems where such bases are not strictly orthonormal. We conclude this report with an appendix outlining the rules governing the use of geometric vectors and related constructs in our system. These rules apply consistently across various notations, including those used for Euclidean spaces with orthonormal bases.

Contextual linear bandits represent a significant area of research with extensive applications in industries such as advertising, healthcare, and education. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of achieving optimal learning rates for regression without the idealized setting of i.i.d. contextual distributions, specifically within a realistic scenario where contexts follow a distribution that is i.i.d. but unknown. Focusing on a worst-case analysis of contexts, we define a novel loss function characterized by an rank-like attribute and a rank-like attribute associated with the loss itself. Our theoretical findings reveal that the sample complexity required to attain optimal learning rates is directly proportional to this rank-like attribute of the loss. Specifically, for a $p$-dimensional linear parameter space with rank-like attribute $r$, the optimal learning rate is given by $C(\log T)/\sqrt{T}$, where $T$ represents the time horizon and $C$ is a constant. We establish an upper bound on sample complexity that aligns with this optimal rate. Furthermore, in a scenario where the context distribution is both i.i.d. and known, we derive an upper bound of $C\sqrt{p\log T}/\sqrt{T}$ for the sample complexity to achieve this specific environment. Notably, our analysis requires no prior assumptions regarding the context distribution other than it being i.i.d., and we do not need to know a specific distributional form to prove the lower bounds concerning the time horizon $T$ and the rank-like attribute $r$. Finally, in a distributed context-linear bandit problem, we examine learning between two agents in an offline-online setup without sharing the context distribution: one agent operates online while the other utilizes an offline dataset. These results confirm that the sample complexity for the offline agent to reach the optimal learning rate of the online agent is at least $T^{2/3}, p$, and $r$, respectively. However, our derived upper bounds indicate that the offline agent can achieve the same optimal learning rate as the online agent with significantly lower complexity: $\min(T^{2/3}, T/\log T), p + 2$, and $r + 2$. The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and growth, dust itself may be impacted by the instability. Specifically, settling dust reduces local gas surface density, which in turn affects cooling rates and VSI stability. Furthermore, as dust grows, its size-dependent settling becomes more pronounced, potentially altering cooling and VSI activity in the outer disk regions. This study employs 2D global simulations to investigate how dust evolution and coagulation modulate VSI onset in the outer parts of protoplanetary disks. Our results indicate that dust growth and size-dependent settling can delay VSI activation; for instance, when the stopping time at 10 AU reaches $0.01$, the instability is suppressed at velocities of $0.1$ times the local Keplerian speed. Additionally, we find that dust growth and coagulation in the  mm size range can lower the $\alpha$ parameter from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-4}$ at a stopping time of $0.01$ at 10 AU. These outcomes suggest that dust evolution in the outer disk regions can mitigate turbulence caused by the VSI. Consequently, future research should focus on the interplay between dust growth, coagulation, and the VSI. Such investigations are crucial for clarifying dust evolution processes and the sequential formation of small and large planets in the outer regions of these disks. To model dust evolution effectively in the outer zones, it is necessary to account for drift, size-dependent settling, and coagulation, as these mechanisms are interconnected. This study examines harmonic functions defined on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons, a class of shrinking Ricci soliton manifolds characterized by uniform scalar curvature. We establish a Liouville theorem on such manifolds and its generalized versions, demonstrating that under specific conditions, any harmonic function must be constant. As a consequence, we apply these findings to the stability analysis of elliptic operators on gradient shrinking solitons with the same uniformity assumption. The principal result connects the Bochner technique with the maximum principle, offering a novel approach to deriving estimates for the Hessian on gradient shrinking solitons with uniform scalar curvature. Furthermore, we consider an elliptic operator constructed from the Laplacian and the Hamiltonian flow, applying the established Liouville result to evaluate its associated eigenvalue problem. These applications highlight the utility of the new Liouville theorem in addressing eigenvalue issues for constructed elliptic operators on gradient shrinking solitons with uniform scalar curvature. The Bochner method and its applications remain a significant area of research in geometric analysis; consequently, this work aims to develop a new Liouville principle based on this technique, which may prove valuable in other geometric contexts. Our findings also rely on the maximum principle and its extensions, particularly the minimum action required to create a bump and its generalizations, as seen in recent literature. Additional related concepts include the mean curvature flow, special holonomy, and their interconnections with the Liouville theorem and its broader implications. Ultimately, this research aligns with ongoing efforts to explore the maximum principle, its generalized forms, and their applications across various areas of geometric analysis. Readers interested in the maximum principle, its extensions, and related topics—such as mean curvature flow, special holonomy, and Liouville theorems—may find this work and its references particularly relevant and engaging. On the technical front, our approach utilizes standard tools from differential geometry, including Bochner formulas and their variants, alongside analyses of gradient and Laplacian evolutions along gradient solitons and their generalized frameworks.

The rise of outsourced AI models has introduced new attack surfaces, making AI systems vulnerable to various backdoor attacks. Recently, neural network-based dynamic backdoors have emerged as a significant threat because they require zero changes to the model architecture during activation. These attacks utilize global mean pooling layers to activate the backend. However, this specific layer offers limited representation, constraining the design of effective dynamic backdoors. In this paper, we introduce a more potent dynamic backdoor by incorporating a complex network of global mean pooling layers. Through extensive numerical experiments, we successfully activated this backdoor against state-of-the-art image classification models, achieving an activation success rate of 99.02% with an overhead reduction of nearly three orders of magnitude compared to static backdoors. Furthermore, we activated this backdoor in a real-world scenario against an open-source image model, demonstrating a 98.77% success rate. These results highlight the significant security risks posed by our proposed dynamic backdoor. To mitigate these risks, we offer practical countermeasures and validate their effectiveness through activation experiments. Our source code will be made available at: https://github.com/SDS-UOC/DBD-GlobalMean. We anticipate that this research will help security communities develop more robust AI systems by exposing the limitations and dangers of global mean pooling layers. Specifically, our findings suggest that deep global mean pooling layer structures should be avoided in real-world image models to prevent dynamic backdoor activations. Additionally, our results support the notion that a 2D convolutional layer followed by a global mean pooling layer—commonly recommended as a safe alternative—may not always be secure against such attacks. Ultimately, further investigation is required to create effective countermeasures against dynamic backdoors in real-world applications.

This study examines the challenge of Federated Learning (FL) under Data Distribution (NID) heterogeneity, a scenario where models fail to generalize to sites with distinct data distributions. Unlike existing approaches that rely on deep architectures or task-specific methods like Meta-Gradient, our proposed method requires no prior knowledge of the underlying NID issues at various sites. We introduce Learn-for-Wandering, a random walk-based algorithm effective in NID heterogeneous environments. Empirical results from both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions. Additionally, the random walk mechanism provides a natural exploration capability, making the method well-suited for applications such as recommendation systems. To the best of our knowledge, this work constitutes the first investigation into random walk-based learning within Federated Learning from heterogeneous data. Further, we establish a theoretical framework showing that the Learn-for-Wandering strategy achieves optimal convergence rates in Statistical Learning, and consequently, in FL, regardless of NID heterogeneity. Codes are accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1009/Random-Walk-FL.

Pixel-level annotation scarcity remains a significant challenge in medical image segmentation. To address this, we investigate regularization strategies that leverage data distributions both inside and outside the segmentation mask. Specifically, we introduce an awkwardly simple consistency regularization approach for an encoder-based segmentation model trained on semi-supervised data. This method enforces a constraint where the segmentation predicted by an consistency regularized test image, augmented with the identity mapping, must match the true mask. We validate this framework using three medical image datasets: ISBI-2017, PASCAL-PCAM, and a heart failure dataset. Historically, these have been viewed as a spectrum of effects explained by single "nonlocal" resources, typically measured by the strength of correlations that breach a specific Bell inequality. Conversely, we demonstrate that genuine nonlocality, as shown by Bell inequality violations, is actually a separate resource arising from a truly unique mechanism: single-particle entanglement. We establish this by proving a "single-particle Bell inequality," which is breached when a system exhibits genuine nonlocality. Using this framework, we show that genuine nonlocality provides an optimal strategy for violating the CHSH inequality, and we confirm experimentally that single-particle entanglement can violate this inequality to achieve the maximum possible nonlocality. Furthermore, we prove that both hiding single-particle entanglement in mixed states and performing measurements on such states are necessary to generate genuine nonlocality. Finally, we argue that single-particle entanglement is the mechanism behind "spooky action-at-a-distance," as it allows for the coexistence of instantaneous effects—like steering and apparent signal transmission—at a distance with local correlations, even when no underlying hidden variables are present. These findings reveal that genuine nonlocality and single-particle entanglement are distinct, complementary resources, a conclusion supported by the fact that single-particle entanglement can violate Bell inequalities even when no genuine nonlocality is present. Our results indicate that genuine nonlocality serves as a witness for single-particle entanglement, much like how Bell inequality violations witness quantum nonlocality, and we provide an operational method for maximizing single-particle entanglement using genuine nonlocality. Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are a potent class of deep neural networks widely adopted for sequence analysis tasks, such as video identification. Second, we designed a hardware architecture specifically for the HT matrix multiplication operation, enabling a novel "straight-through companding" inference workflow where LSTM layers perform standard matrix multiplication via memory access, while HT layers execute multiplication and folding operations in real-time. Test results with high-definition (720p) videos demonstrate that an HT-LSTM model, nine times smaller than a conventional LSTM, processed by our hardware achieves a 30.7× speedup over an uncompressed LSTM running on FPGAs and a 100× speedup over CPU implementations. Additionally, experiments with 4K videos indicate that the HT-LSTM architecture and hardware can effectively handle even higher resolutions. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the initial co-design of an algorithm and hardware specifically tailored for HT networks. The proposed algorithm and hardware design for HT-LSTM are open-sourced at: https://github.com/HTLSTM/HTLSTM_And_Hardware_CoDesign.

Hypothesis testing is a fundamental component of cognitive science, with Bayes factors serving as a primary method for evaluating hypotheses based on data. Although widely adopted, significant uncertainties remain regarding the optimal strategy for calculating Bayes factors to draw reliable conclusions. This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of different strategies for utilizing Bayes factors to assess hypotheses in cognitive science. The results indicate that a specific strategy offers the greatest robustness. Furthermore, the practical application of this optimal approach demands high precision in data collection, a requirement that can be satisfied through automated data analysis workflows integrated with robotic laboratories. Such an integration represents a promising direction for the future of cognitive science. Additionally, this work includes a detailed review of the prior distributions employed by the JASP Bayesian t-test module.

Detecting magnetic fields with SQUIDs has long served as the gold standard for high-sensitivity measurements. We propose a novel approach to achieve comparable sensitivity with an atomic interferometer, leveraging the Meissner effect of superconductors to extend detection range. Demonstrating this concept, we constructed a device combining a 350-mm tall lead bucket, filled with liquid lead, and an atomic interferometer operating at 102 Tesella -256 Celsius. This system detected local magnetic field changes as small as 1.4 nT per root Hz within a 150-mm radius, covering the sensitivity spectrum found with SQUIDs. Given that atomic interferometers are compatible with larger baselines, this method could potentially offer even higher sensitivity. Furthermore, the system functions as a magnetometer with significant seismic stability, as the atomic fall tube is effectively isolated from ground vibrations by the superconducting bucket. This seismic independence opens possibilities for detecting magnetic field fluctuations induced by seismic waves along the fall tube's direction. Potential applications include magnetic sensing, gravity mapping via the equivalence principle, and seismic sensing for disaster mitigation or nuclear detection. To our knowledge, this work represents the first demonstration of atomic interferometry in the microwave domain; achieving this required developing new technologies for cooling, containing, and detecting atoms at ultra-low temperatures.

Consequently, the Poincaré-Bendixson theorem is not directly applicable to fractional-order systems, necessitating the development of alternative methods to investigate global dynamics in these models. This study presents a novel inverse problem involving the 3D structural acoustic coupling between an active shell and an enclosing cavity. Using an experimental setup, we attempted to identify the boundary conditions of the cavity by measuring the shell's vibration modes and their associated acoustic modes. The inverse procedure relied on a Bayesian optimization algorithm to adjust the cavity's boundary conditions so that the simulated natural frequencies matched those experimentally obtained. The results successfully recovered the known boundary conditions of the acoustic cavity, with a mean error of less than 5%. To address the issue of multiple local minima during optimization, we proposed an strategy to restrict the search space for the boundary conditions based on the characteristics of the eigenmodes. Additionally, we demonstrated that this inverse method can detect modifications to the actual boundary conditions.

We introduce the simplest non-invertible seesaw model extending the standard scoto-model, termed the easiest scoto-seesaw model. This framework unifies three key mechanisms: seesaw generation, dark matter (DM) stabilization, and mass generation for the $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry. Within this model, DM stabilization occurs via exchange of a singlet scalar and right-handed neutrinos, while the right-handed neutrinos simultaneously generate the seesaw mechanism. We conduct a comprehensive phenomenological analysis, detailing a strategy to ensure vacuum stability, designing optimized search strategies for dark sector processes at the LHC, and examining dark matter direct detection signatures. Our findings indicate that the singlet scalar mediates thermal freeze-out, which can be suppressed by the $N_3$ particle through co-annihilation. To achieve the desired relic density, the mass of the $N_3$ must exceed that of the mediating scalar, $\mu_2$, by approximately a factor of two. In this configuration, the neutrino mass matrix acquires two negative eigenvalues, giving rise to two heavy seesaw states, while the DM mass matrix yields one positive and one negative eigenvalue; the latter corresponds to our stable dark matter candidate. We anticipate that this model's distinctive predictions—specifically three $s$-channel resonances and two DM states—will serve as a focal point for future research. Our results suggest that the standard seesaw mechanism, right-neutrino doublet exchange, and DM stabilization through CO-ANNIHILATION and FUNNEL processes can all be realized with neutrino masses and mixing angles aligning with current experimental constraints. The model's parameter space and predicted neutronic properties are illustrated in the paper's three figures and summarized table. Complementary discussions regarding neutronic characteristics, dark matter properties, and phenomenology are provided in the accompanying files. Mathematically, we employ the spectral decomposition of symmetric matrices to analyze mass matrices and determine their eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Metaphorically, we envision the dark matter as a "lonely" stable particle residing in the cosmic dark sector, with its "life history" dictated by CO-ANNIHILATION and FUNNEL mechanisms. Physically, the mass hierarchy follows $M_{N_3} > \mu_2 > M_{\rm DM}$, where the dark matter is identified as the lighter eigenvalue of the DM mass matrix.
